subject: Business Models
title: Franchise Licensing
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Franchise Licensing.

hook.text: McDonald's doesn't flip burgers. It licenses its brand, system, and playbook to 40,000 franchisees.

buildup.text: Franchisees pay an initial fee ($45,000) plus 4% of gross sales monthly. McDonald's also owns the real estate.

discovery.text: McDonald's earns more from real estate rent than from franchise fees. The food is secondary.

twist.text: Franchisees bear all the operational risk. McDonald's collects fees whether the location succeeds or fails.

climax.text: Franchise licensing lets brands scale globally without capital risk. 36,000 of 40,000 stores are franchised.

punchline.text: McDonald's is a real estate company disguised as a restaurant.

quiz.question: What is McDonald's largest revenue source?

details.summary: Franchise licensing grants independent operators the right to use a brand name, business system, and operational playbook in exchange for upfront fees and ongoing royalties. McDonald's collects 4% of sales from each franchise location plus rent on company-owned real estate.
details.whyItMatters: Franchising enabled rapid scaling of business models without requiring the franchisor's own capital. It generates high-margin recurring revenue from royalties while franchisees bear the operational and financial risks of individual locations.
takeaways: Operators pay fees and royalties for the right to use a proven business system
Franchisors earn recurring revenue while franchisees bear operational risk
Franchise models scale rapidly using other people's capital and labor

faq.question: How do franchise fee structures typically work?
faq.answer: Franchisees pay an initial franchise fee of $20,000 to $100,000 for the right to operate. Ongoing royalties range from 4% to 8% of gross sales. Marketing fund contributions add 1% to 4%. Some franchisors also earn revenue from required supply purchases and real estate leases.

faq.question: What are the biggest risks of the franchise model?
faq.answer: Brand damage from poor-performing franchisees, legal disputes over territory rights and operational standards, reputational risks from labor practices at franchised locations, and the challenge of maintaining quality consistency across hundreds or thousands of independent operators.
